title: Climate change misinformation
text:
And for climate change specifically?
On average across eight countries, 25% said they had seen false or misleading information about climate change in the past week. (Ejaz et al., 2025)

Ejaz, Mukherjee & Fletcher 2025, Reuters Institute “Climate Change and News Audiences Report 2024” (DOI 10.60625/risj-vsjy-zm64, 8 countries: Brazil, France, Germany, India, Japan, Pakistan, UK, USA). Report text: “On average across eight countries, 25% of respondents in 2024 say that they had ‘personally seen, read, or heard’” false or misleading information about climate change in the past week; “This is very similar to the 27% figure from 2023 and 2022”; highest in “India (43%)”, lowest in “UK (17%) and Japan (16%)”. Their caveat: “these are perceptions and do not necessarily reflect the prevalence”.

title: Climate change misinformation
text:
1. Recognising techniques
You do not need to know every false claim. Most misinformation relies on a small set of rhetorical techniques, and those can be learned.

One list of five goes by the acronym FLICC: fake experts, logical fallacies, impossible expectations, cherry picking, conspiracy theories. (Cook, 2020)

Cook, J. (2020). Deconstructing climate science denial. In D. Holmes & L. M. Richardson (Eds.), Research Handbook on Communicating Climate Change. Edward Elgar. DOI 10.4337/9781789900408.00014. The five categories in Cook’s own words on Skeptical Science: “Fake experts, Logical fallacies, Impossible expectations, Cherry picking, and Conspiracy theories” (https://skepticalscience.com/history-FLICC-5-techniques-science-denial.html). The five techniques go back to Hoofnagle (2007), the acronym to Cook (2013). A graphic of the full taxonomy is on Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0), a German version (“PLURV”) at klimafakten.de.
Today’s reading lists the strategies of organised disinformation in similar terms (sidebar “Rhetorical strategies of disinformation”): undermine and question the scientific consensus, highlight uncertainty and demand certainty as a condition for action, attack individual scientists, undermine institutions such as peer review, project pseudoscientific alternatives through a network of blogs.

title: Climate change misinformation
text:
The case for calm
What the behavioural data show, in their reading, is “a pattern of low exposure to false and inflammatory content that is concentrated among a narrow fringe with strong motivations to seek out such information” (Budak et al., 2024).

Let us look at some of that data.

Budak, Nyhan, Rothschild, Thorson & Watts 2024, Nature, DOI 10.1038/s41586-024-07417-w. All quotes from the abstract. Their policy recommendation: hold platforms accountable for the tails of the distribution, and demand transparency and data access for researchers.

title: Climate change misinformation
section: It depends on how you measure
text:
It depends on how you measure
In surveys, 58% of people say they have seen misinformation. In content analyses, 23% of items get classified as misinformation. (Altay, 2026b)

How misinformation was identified, and whether at the level of sources or of items, explained more of the differences between estimates than platform or topic.


Most of these estimates come from the US and concern fact-checked “fake news”. Keep that in mind for the reply from the other camp.

Altay et al. 2026 (systematic review, in Zotero, no DOI yet). Abstract: “In behavioural studies, misinformation is a median 1.3% of what people consume online; it reaches 12.0% of people at least once and makes up 13.0% of what they share. In surveys, 57.7% say they have seen misinformation and 19.8% say they have shared it. In content analyses, 23.0% of items are classified as misinformation. How misinformation was identified (by fact-checkers, domain lists, researchers, or classifiers) and at which level (sources or items) explained more of the variance between estimates than what the study was about; platform and topic explained less. […] The top 1% of users account for a median 70% of misinformation sharing or exposure.”
Earlier single studies pointing the same way (Allen et al., 2020; Grinberg et al., 2019; Guess et al., 2019). Grinberg et al. 2019, Science (Twitter, 2016 US election): “Only 1% of individuals accounted for 80% of fake news source exposures, and 0.1% accounted for nearly 80% of fake news sources shared.” Guess, Nagler & Tucker 2019, Science Advances (Facebook): “8.5% of respondents for whom we have linked Facebook data shared at least one such article”. Allen et al. 2020, Science Advances: “fake news comprises only 0.15% of Americans’ daily media diet”, and news of any kind is at most 14.2% of the media diet, with TV about five times online.
Also Vosoughi, Roy & Aral 2018, Science (Vosoughi et al., 2018), the famous finding that on Twitter “falsehoods were 70% more likely to be retweeted than the truth” (about 126,000 stories, about 3 million people, bots spread both at the same rate). Altay, Berriche & Acerbi 2023 (Altay et al., 2023) list as one of six misconceptions that “falsehoods do not spread faster than the truth”: the Vosoughi sample was fact-checked stories, which are selected for being contested, not a random sample of true and false content.
Caveat to say out loud: these estimates mostly come from the US and from fact-checked “fake news”. Climate-specific estimates are rarer, and the definitions matter (see the Ecker reply, next slides).

title: Climate change misinformation
text:
Rejecting specific findings
Given the scientific answer to basic science questions, 95% of US participants accepted it. Among those with no trust in science: 87%. (Pfänder et al., 2025)

People reject the specific claims that conflict with their worldview, while accepting science in general.

Pfänder, Altay, Dubourg & Mercier 2025, Public Understanding of Science. Abstract: “Acceptance of the scientific consensus was very high in the sample as a whole (95.1%), but also in every sub-sample (e.g. no trust in science: 87.3%; complete endorsement of flat Earth theory: 87.2%). This quasi-universal acceptance of basic science suggests that people are motivated to reject specific scientific beliefs, and not science as a whole.”

title: Climate change misinformation
text:
Fact-checking outside the US
In Argentina, Nigeria, South Africa and the UK, fact-checks reduced belief in misinformation by at least 0.59 points on a five-point scale, and most effects were still visible two weeks later. (Porter & Wood, 2021)

The misinformation itself moved beliefs by less than 0.07 points on the same scale.

Lewandowsky, Ecker, Seifert, Schwarz & Cook 2012, Psychological Science in the Public Interest, DOI 10.1177/1529100612451018. The review explains “why retractions of misinformation are so ineffective in memory updating and why efforts to retract misinformation can even backfire and, ironically, increase misbelief.” Ecker et al. 2022, Nature Reviews Psychology, define the effect: belief in misinformation “exerts a lingering influence on people’s reasoning after it has been corrected — an effect known as the continued influence effect.”
Chan, Jones, Hall Jamieson & Albarracín 2017, Psychological Science, DOI 10.1177/0956797617714579: “This meta-analysis (k = 52, N = 6,878) revealed large effects for presenting misinformation (ds = 2.41–3.08), debunking (ds = 1.14–1.33), and the persistence of misinformation in the face of debunking (ds = 0.75–1.06).”
Walter & Murphy 2018, Communication Monographs, DOI 10.1080/03637751.2018.1467564: “corrective messages have a moderate influence on belief in misinformation (r = .35); however, it is more difficult to correct for misinformation in the context of politics (r = .15) and marketing (r = .18) than health (r = .27). … Rebuttals (r = .38) are more effective than forewarnings (r = .16)”.
Walter, Cohen, Holbert & Morag 2020, Political Communication, DOI 10.1080/10584609.2019.1668894: “(k = 30, N = 20,963). Fact-checking has a significantly positive overall influence on political beliefs (d = 0.29), but the effects gradually weaken when using ‘truth scales,’ refuting only parts of a claim, and fact-checking campaign-related statements.”
Porter & Wood 2021, PNAS, DOI 10.1073/pnas.2104235118 (Argentina, Nigeria, South Africa, UK, 22 fact-checks): “fact-checks reduced belief in misinformation by at least 0.59 points on a 5-point scale. Exposure to misinformation, however, only increased false beliefs by less than 0.07 points on the same scale.” and “most effects still apparent more than 2 wk later”.

title: Climate change misinformation
text:
Beyond the individual
Individual-level tools have modest effects that decay. Two structural measures remain.

Hold platforms accountable for the narrow fringe of users among whom, as we saw in part 3, exposure to misinformation concentrates. (Budak et al., 2024)


Address the organised supply of doubt from part 1.

Altay, Lyons & Modirrousta-Galian 2024, Communications Psychology, N = 3,919. Abstract: “Skepticism-enhancing tips, Trust-inducing tips, and a mix of both tips, increased participants’ sharing and accuracy discernment. […] the Trust-inducing tips increased trust in traditional media.”
Budak et al. 2024: “we recommend holding platforms accountable for facilitating exposure to false and extreme content in the tails of the distribution, where consumption is highest and the risk of real-world harm is greatest.”

title: Climate change misinformation
text:
The Exxon case



Protest sign in Washington, DC, 2015. Photo: Johnny Silvercloud, Wikimedia Commons



Say it, do not show it: in 2015, journalists showed that the oil company’s own scientists had understood climate change since the late 1970s. Introduce the company first: Exxon, since 1999 ExxonMobil, the successor of Rockefeller’s Standard Oil, for decades the largest publicly traded oil company in the world. The story became public through the InsideClimate News series “Exxon: The Road Not Taken” (2015, Pulitzer finalist, https://www.pulitzer.org/finalists/insideclimate-news) and the hashtag #ExxonKnew on the sign.
What the company knew: Supran, Rahmstorf & Oreskes 2023, Science, DOI 10.1126/science.abk0063, evaluated “all available global warming projections documented by—and in many cases modeled by—Exxon and ExxonMobil Corp scientists between 1977 and 2003. We find that most of their projections accurately forecast warming that is consistent with subsequent observations. Their projections were also consistent with, and at least as skillful as, those of independent academic and government models.” In numbers: “63 to 83% of the climate projections reported by ExxonMobil scientists were accurate”, average projected warming “0.20° ± 0.04°C per decade”, warming predicted to become detectable “in the year 2000 ± 5”.
The 1982 internal memo with the CO2 projection chart is at https://www.climatefiles.com/exxonmobil/1982-memo-to-exxon-management-about-CO2-greenhouse-effect. Tobia’s slides 9 and 10 quote three Exxon documents (1977, 1982, 1997) in French. I did not verify their English wording, so they are not on the slide.

title: Climate change misinformation
text:
Merchants of doubt





Oreskes & Conway (2010)



A small group of senior physicists, among them Fred Seitz, a former president of the US National Academy of Sciences, founded the George C. Marshall Institute, a think tank that from 1989 on campaigned against climate science.
ExxonMobil was among its funders. (Oreskes & Conway, 2010)


Before that, Seitz had been a paid consultant to the tobacco company R.J. Reynolds, helping to decide how its research money was spent, at a time when the industry’s aim was to keep the health risks of smoking looking uncertain.
Oreskes and Conway stress that nothing in this story was illegal or hidden. The campaigns were run in the open, by scientists with political connections and a conviction that environmental regulation would lead to socialism.
Oreskes & Conway, Merchants of Doubt: How a Handful of Scientists Obscured the Truth on Issues from Tobacco Smoke to Global Warming (Bloomsbury Press, 2010). Naomi Oreskes is a historian of science at Harvard, Erik Conway a historian at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory. Their own summary (merchantsofdoubt.org): “a loose-knit group of high-level scientists, with extensive political connections, ran effective campaigns to mislead the public and deny well-established scientific knowledge over four decades.”
The people: Fred Seitz (physicist, worked on the atomic bomb, president of the National Academy of Sciences 1962 to 1969, president of Rockefeller University 1968 to 1978), Fred Singer (physicist, space and satellite research), William Nierenberg (physicist, former director of the Scripps Institution of Oceanography) and Robert Jastrow (founder of NASA’s Goddard Institute for Space Studies). All fiercely anti-communist. Seitz, Jastrow and Nierenberg founded the George C. Marshall Institute in 1984 to defend Reagan’s Strategic Defense Initiative. From 1989 the institute turned to “a critical examination of the scientific basis for global climate change policy”, starting with a Nierenberg report attributing warming to solar activity. A 1990 report by Jastrow, Nierenberg and Seitz informed the first Bush administration’s position. The institute received 715,000 dollars from ExxonMobil between 1998 and 2008 (Guardian, 30 September 2008). It closed in 2015.
The tobacco link: shortly before his retirement from Rockefeller University in 1979, Seitz became a permanent consultant to R.J. Reynolds, advising its medical research programme until 1988 and helping to allocate research funding. Seitz’s own defence: “The money was all spent on basic science, medical science.” Oreskes and Conway’s reading: he “used normal uncertainties of scientific evidence to spread doubt about the harmfulness of tobacco smoke”. In 1994 Seitz wrote that “there is no good scientific evidence that passive inhalation is truly dangerous under normal circumstances.”
The Lewandowsky reading makes the same comparison: contrarian rhetoric “resembles the tobacco industry’s campaigns to undermine the medical evidence about the health risks from smoking” (section 3).

title: Climate change misinformation
text:
Techniques online
A second list, written for online misinformation, names six techniques: impersonation, emotional content, polarisation, conspiracy, discrediting, trolling. (Roozenbeek & van der Linden, 2019)

It overlaps with FLICC, and we will meet it again in the inoculation games below.

title: Climate change misinformation
section: Has it worked? What the public believes
text:
Has it worked? What the public believes
In the EU, the share who say climate change is mostly natural rose from 26% in 2021 to 35% in 2024. (European Commission, Directorate-General for Research and Innovation, 2021, 2025; Rutjens et al., 2022)

Is misinformation the cause? That is what two camps of researchers disagree about.

Eurobarometer, “European citizens’ knowledge and attitudes towards science and technology”, 2021 (DOI 10.2775/071577) and Special Eurobarometer 557, 2025 (DOI 10.2777/6040908). The 26% and 35% figures are the ones used in Jan’s Ambizione research plan (research_plan.qmd, “Overall objective”), where the item is described as the share who say climate change is mostly natural instead of human-caused. Check the exact item wording in the 2025 report before quoting it to students.
Rutjens et al. 2022, Social Psychological and Personality Science, DOI 10.1177/19485506211001329, “Science skepticism across 24 countries”: climate scepticism was related to political conservatism mostly in North America, and spirituality and religiosity predicted other forms of scepticism (vaccines, evolution) in more countries.
Tobia’s slide 5 shows a world map of the share who think climate change is caused mostly by humans. Its source is not given on the slide (it looks like the Yale “International Public Opinion on Climate Change” report). Use it only after checking the source.

title: Climate change misinformation
text:
Figure in Supran et al. (2023). (A) A 1982 internal Exxon projection with observed CO2 (blue) and temperature (red) added. (B) Projections from seven internal memos and five peer-reviewed papers, 1977 to 2003 (grey), against observed warming (red). (C) A 1977 internal graph of a CO2-induced “super-interglacial”.
The lines in (A) are Exxon’s 1982 projections of CO2 and temperature, and the coloured observations run along them. The company’s scientists were right.

title: Climate change misinformation
text:
What today’s reading concludes

Climate change challenges our cognitive abilities and the worldviews of many.
Communication takes place in an environment of adversity.
Information about the scientific consensus, and about why climate change occurs, can enhance acceptance of science.
Culturally aligned messages and messengers are more likely to succeed.
Inoculation can defang misinformation before it is encountered.

Summary points, shortened, from Lewandowsky (2021)

Lewandowsky 2021, “Summary points”, verbatim: “1. Climate change challenges our cognitive abilities and the worldviews of many. 2. Because addressing climate change has serious economic and political implications, any communication takes place in an environment of adversity. 3. Providing information about climate change, in particular about the scientific consensus and explanations of why it occurs, can enhance people’s acceptance of science. 4. Culturally aligned messages and messengers are more likely to be successful. 5. Through a process known as inoculation, climate misinformation can be rebutted or, ideally, defanged before it is encountered.”
Where today’s lecture went beyond the reading: the prevalence estimates (section 3), the mixed evidence on inoculation after 2021 (Spampatti et al. 2023, the signal-detection reanalyses), and Part III on the information ecosystem.

title: Climate change misinformation
section: Do such techniques make false claims more convincing?
text:
Do such techniques make false claims more convincing?
Not much. In five EU countries, adding most of these techniques to a claim about climate change made people agree with it less. (Nohlen & Bruns, 2025)

The main reason: people agreed less with true claims written in this style.

Give one-line definitions orally. Tobia’s slides 23 to 29 define them (in French, after Roozenbeek & van der Linden 2019): discrediting deflects criticism by attacking the source, conspiracy explains events through a small malicious elite, trolling provokes a reaction with bait, polarisation amplifies existing tensions between groups, impersonation fakes accounts or identities, emotional content plays on fear, anger or empathy.
Roozenbeek & van der Linden 2019, Palgrave Communications, the “Bad News” game by Jon Roozenbeek and Sander van der Linden. The six badges in the game are discredit, conspiracy, trolling, polarization, impersonation, emotion. Their later inoculation videos target five related techniques, Roozenbeek et al. 2022, Science Advances: “We developed five short videos that inoculate people against manipulation techniques commonly used in misinformation: emotionally manipulative language, incoherence, false dichotomies, scapegoating, and ad hominem attacks.”
Nohlen et al. 2025 (preprint, in Zotero). Abstract: “In an online experiment with 5,121 participants from five EU countries, we examined how seven persuasion techniques influence agreement and perceived persuasiveness of climate change disinformation and factual claims. Persuasion techniques reduced agreement overall, mainly by lowering agreement with true claims. Some techniques (e.g., appeal to authority, black-and-white fallacy) increased agreement with false claims.”
The nuance: rhetorical tricks are not magic. People are somewhat sensitive to them, and the tricks can backfire for true information.

title: Climate change misinformation
text:
Two weeks ago





Photo: ETH Zürich, D-USYS



Reto Knutti told us what it is like to be a climate scientist in public: he is attacked personally and discredited, rather than argued with.


Recap of the guest lecture in week 7 (27.10.): the personal attacks, the attempts to discredit him as a person rather than engage with the science, and how he deals with it.
Today’s reading has a section on exactly this, “Disinformation versus scientists” (Lewandowsky 2021, section 3.3): “Several researchers have suggested that the constant barrage of public criticism and attacks on individual scientists has induced the scientific community to exercise undue caution or to ‘err on the side of least drama’.” And: “interviews with researchers have revealed that some forms of contrarian activities, such as the use of freedom-of-information requests, have led to changes in how scientists communicate and have imposed an additional work burden that draws time away from research.”

title: Climate change misinformation
text:
Not an isolated experience





Mann & Hotez (2025)



Climate and health action are “hampered by a common threat: politically and ideologically motivated opposition to science”.


Michael Mann, climate scientist, and Peter Hotez, vaccine researcher, two scientists who have “spent the last twenty years on the front lines of the battle to convey accurate, reliable, and trustworthy information about science in the face of determined and nihilistic opposition”. Today is about the first three forces, and about what psychology can say about the audience.
Mann & Hotez 2025, Science Under Siege: How to Fight the Five Most Powerful Forces That Threaten Our World, PublicAffairs, 368 pages, published 9 September 2025. Quotes from the publisher’s description (Hachette Book Group page): “From pandemics to the climate crisis, humanity faces tougher challenges than ever. […] But our efforts to effectively tackle these existential crises are now hampered by a common threat: politically and ideologically motivated opposition to science. Michael E. Mann and Peter J. Hotez are two of the most respected and well-known scientists in the world and have spent the last twenty years on the front lines of the battle to convey accurate, reliable, and trustworthy information about science in the face of determined and nihilistic opposition. In this powerful manifesto, they reveal the five main forces threatening science: plutocrats, pros, petrostates, phonies, and the press.”
Mann himself has been a target of organised attacks on climate scientists for two decades.
Bridge to the lecture: plutocrats, pros and petrostates are the supply side, Part I. The audience, what reaches it and what can be done about it, is Part II. Whether all of this matters, and the role of the press, the fifth force, is Part III.

title: Climate change misinformation
text:
What decision makers think

Figure C in World Economic Forum (2024)
In 2024, the World Economic Forum asked its network of experts and decision makers to rank global risks by severity. Over a two-year horizon, “misinformation and disinformation” came first, ahead of extreme weather events. Over ten years, extreme weather came first and misinformation fifth. The ranking says something about how worried elites are, not necessarily about how big the problem is. That is the question of this part: does misinformation matter, and in what way?

title: Climate change misinformation
section: Has the supply of doubt worked? What the public believes
text:
Has the supply of doubt worked? What the public believes
In the EU, the share who say climate change is mostly natural rose from 26% in 2021 to 35% in 2024. (European Commission, Directorate-General for Research and Innovation, 2021, 2025; Rutjens et al., 2022)

Is misinformation the cause? That is what two camps of researchers disagree about.

Eurobarometer, “European citizens’ knowledge and attitudes towards science and technology”, 2021 (DOI 10.2775/071577) and Special Eurobarometer 557, 2025 (DOI 10.2777/6040908). The 26% and 35% figures are the ones used in Jan’s Ambizione research plan (research_plan.qmd, “Overall objective”), where the item is described as the share who say climate change is mostly natural instead of human-caused. Check the exact item wording in the 2025 report before quoting it to students.
Rutjens et al. 2022, Social Psychological and Personality Science, DOI 10.1177/19485506211001329, “Science skepticism across 24 countries”: climate scepticism was related to political conservatism mostly in North America, and spirituality and religiosity predicted other forms of scepticism (vaccines, evolution) in more countries.
Tobia’s slide 5 shows a world map of the share who think climate change is caused mostly by humans. Its source is not given on the slide (it looks like the Yale “International Public Opinion on Climate Change” report). Use it only after checking the source.

title: Climate change misinformation
section: Accepting science in general, rejecting specific findings
text:
Accepting science in general, rejecting specific findings
When US participants were shown the scientific answer to basic science questions, 95% accepted it. Among those who said they had no trust in science at all, 87% still accepted it. (Pfänder et al., 2025)

People reject the specific claims that conflict with their worldview, while accepting science in general.

Pfänder, Altay, Dubourg & Mercier 2025, Public Understanding of Science. Abstract: “Acceptance of the scientific consensus was very high in the sample as a whole (95.1%), but also in every sub-sample (e.g. no trust in science: 87.3%; complete endorsement of flat Earth theory: 87.2%). This quasi-universal acceptance of basic science suggests that people are motivated to reject specific scientific beliefs, and not science as a whole.”

title: Climate change misinformation
text:
Who is vulnerable? Age
Only 8.5% of US Facebook users shared any fake news in 2016. (A. Guess et al., 2019)

Users over 65 shared nearly seven times as much as the youngest age group. (Brashier & Schacter, 2020)

Pennycook & Rand 2019, Cognition, DOI 10.1016/j.cognition.2018.06.011, “two studies (total N = 3446 Mechanical Turk workers)”. Their review in Pennycook & Rand 2021, Trends in Cognitive Sciences (Pennycook & Rand, 2021): “poor truth discernment is associated with lack of careful reasoning and relevant knowledge, and the use of heuristics such as familiarity. Furthermore, there is a substantial disconnect between what people believe and what they share on social media.”
Rathje, Roozenbeek, Van Bavel & van der Linden 2023, Nature Human Behaviour, n = 3,364. Abstract: “Financial incentives improved accuracy and reduced partisan bias in judgements of headlines by about 30%, primarily by increasing the perceived accuracy of true news from the opposing party (d = 0.47). […] incentives closed the gap in accuracy between conservatives and liberals by 52%.” The two accounts are not mutually exclusive: people who reason more spot more falsehoods, and people motivated to be accurate reason more.
Age: Guess, Nagler & Tucker 2019: “users over 65 shared nearly seven times as many articles from fake news domains as the youngest age group”. Brashier & Schacter 2020, Current Directions: “Older adults are especially susceptible—they shared the most fake news during the 2016 U.S. election.” and “cognitive declines cannot fully explain older adults’ engagement with fake news.” Digital literacy, social goals and trust seem to play a role.

title: Climate change misinformation
section: The backfire effect, which mostly does not appear
text:
The backfire effect, which mostly does not appear
An influential 2010 study found that corrections could increase a misperception among the group most committed to it. (Nyhan & Reifler, 2010)

Later attempts to reproduce this, across 52 issues and more than 10,000 participants, “found no corrections capable of triggering backfire”. (Wood & Porter, 2019)

Nyhan & Reifler 2010, Political Behavior, DOI 10.1007/s11109-010-9112-2. Abstract: “We conducted four experiments … corrections frequently fail to reduce misperceptions among the targeted ideological group. We also document several instances of a ‘backfire effect’ in which corrections actually increase misperceptions among the group in question.”
Wood & Porter 2019, Political Behavior, DOI 10.1007/s11109-018-9443-y. “we found no corrections capable of triggering backfire”. Five experiments with more than 10,000 participants and 52 issues (paraphrase). The Debunking Handbook 2020 summarises: “backfire effects occur only occasionally and the risk of occurrence is lower in most situations than once thought.”
Two kinds of backfire were feared: the worldview backfire effect (this slide) and the familiarity backfire effect (repeating the myth strengthens it, see the illusory-truth slide in the backup). Both have little empirical support today. Message for communicators: do not be afraid to correct. Fear of backfire kept many people from debunking at all.

title: Climate change misinformation
section: Debunking many people at once: dialogues with an AI
text:
Debunking many people at once: dialogues with an AI
A short personalised conversation with an AI reduced belief in conspiracy theories by about 20%, for at least two months. (Costello et al., 2024)

“Many conspiracy theory believers can revise their views if presented with sufficiently compelling evidence.”

Costello, Pennycook & Rand 2024, Science, DOI 10.1126/science.adq1814. Abstract: “we leveraged developments in generative artificial intelligence and engaged 2190 conspiracy believers in personalized evidence-based dialogues with GPT-4 Turbo. The intervention reduced conspiracy belief by ~20%. The effect remained 2 months later, generalized across a wide range of conspiracy theories, and occurred even among participants with deeply entrenched beliefs.”
We saw this study in week 4 under “revisiting the deficit model”. It fits here too: tailored, evidence-based correction works, and facts are not useless. Today’s reading, summary point 3: “Providing information about climate change, in particular about the scientific consensus and explanations of why it occurs, can enhance people’s acceptance of science.”

title: Climate change misinformation
text:
Comparing interventions in one experiment
One large study compared nine interventions on 33,233 participants: “a wide variety of interventions can improve discernment”, that is, the ability to tell true from false news. (Fazio et al., 2024, preprint)

The effects are real but modest, and they were measured only minutes after the intervention.

Pennycook, Epstein, Mosleh, Arechar, Eckles & Rand 2021, Nature, DOI 10.1038/s41586-021-03344-2. Abstract: “four survey experiments and a field experiment on Twitter; the results show that subtly shifting attention to accuracy increases the quality of news that people subsequently share.” From the preprint (osf.io/3n9u8): in Study 1, whether a headline was true or false made a 55.9 percentage point difference to accuracy ratings but only 5.9 points to sharing intentions, which is the “disconnect” the intervention exploits. The field experiment messaged 5,379 Twitter users who had previously shared links to Breitbart or Infowars.
A climate example: Lutzke et al. 2019, Global Environmental Change (n = 2,750), found that simple critical-thinking guidelines reduced the likelihood to trust, like and share fake news about climate change on Facebook, with small effect sizes. Today’s reading cites this study as an extension of inoculation towards critical thinking.
Fazio et al. 2024 (preprint, in Zotero), N = 33,233. Abstract: “The current megastudy with 33,233 US-based participants tests nine prominent misinformation interventions in an identical setting using true, false, and misleading health and political news headlines. We find that a wide variety of interventions can improve discernment between true versus false or misleading information during accuracy and sharing judgments.” The interventions include accuracy nudges, digital literacy tips, inoculation and debunking.

title: Climate change misinformation
section: A different goal: trust in true news
text:
A different goal: trust in true news
Tips that encouraged trust in reliable news improved people’s ability to tell true from false news as much as tips that encouraged scepticism, and they also increased trust in traditional media. (Altay et al., 2024)

“There is more room to increase the acceptance of true news than to reduce the acceptance of fact-checked false news.” (Pfänder & Altay, 2025)

title: Climate change misinformation
text:
How common are such attacks?
Of 468 climate scientists who answered a voluntary survey in 2023, 39% had experienced online harassment or abuse related to their research. Among those who appear in the media at least once a month, 73% had. (Global Witness, 2023)

Of 321 scientists who answered a voluntary survey after speaking publicly about COVID-19, 15% had received death threats and 22% threats of physical or sexual violence. (Nogrady, 2021)

Global Witness, “Global hating”, 4 April 2023, https://globalwitness.org/en/campaigns/digital-threats/global-hating/introduction/. Verbatim: “Overall, 39% of all scientists polled (183 out of 468) have experienced online harassment or abuse”; “increases to 49% of scientists who have published more than 10 journal articles”; “Of those scientists who are in the media at least once a month (13% of respondents), 73% have experienced abuse”; “8% have received death threats”; “41% of affected scientists polled said their experience had made them less likely to post”. The invitation went to about 24,000 scientists, and the 468 are a voluntary sample, so the shares are not representative. Reported in Nature by Vidal Valero 2023 (Vidal Valero, 2023): “Among the 468 respondents, 39% said they had experienced online harassment or abuse related to their climate research.”
Nogrady 2021, Nature 598, 250–253, DOI 10.1038/d41586-021-02741-x, Nature’s survey of scientists who had spoken to the media about COVID-19: “15% of 321 respondents said they had received death threats”; “22% had received threats of physical or sexual violence”; “more than 40% reported experiencing emotional or psychological distress”; “more than two-thirds of researchers reported negative experiences”.
Michael Mann v. Steyn and Simberg: Mann sued in 2012 over blog posts comparing him to a convicted child abuser and calling his research fraudulent. On 8 February 2024 a Washington, DC jury awarded him 1 dollar in compensatory damages from each writer and punitive damages of 1,000 dollars from Simberg and 1 million dollars from Steyn (AP, 8 February 2024; Tollefson 2024, Nature 626, 698–699, DOI 10.1038/d41586-024-00396-y). In 2025 the judge reduced the award against Steyn to 5,000 dollars, and Mann was ordered to pay about 530,000 dollars in legal fees to the National Review, which had been dropped from the case (Philadelphia Inquirer, 20 March 2025). So: a symbolic win after twelve years, at considerable cost.
Other figures: a German representative survey of about 2,600 researchers (DZHW, 2024) found that 45% had experienced at least one form of hostility, with death threats or threats of violence at about 2%. An Australian survey of 2,086 academics (Peetz et al. 2024) found that 41% had experienced intimidation in the past five years.

title: Climate change misinformation
section: The Exxon case, which you saw last week
text:
The Exxon case, which you saw last week





Protest sign in Washington, DC, 2015. Photo: Johnny Silvercloud, Wikimedia Commons



From 1977 on, Exxon’s own scientists projected the warming accurately. Meanwhile, the company’s published newspaper advertisements intended to cast doubt on it. (Supran et al., 2023; Supran & Oreskes, 2017)


Recap only: Viktoria covered this in week 8 (her slides 19 to 24: the 1977 memo, the Supran et al. 2023 projection chart, the New York Times advertisements, Supran & Oreskes 2017). One minute, then move on to what is new, the playbook and the people behind it.
Say it, do not show it: in 2015, journalists showed that the oil company’s own scientists had understood climate change since the late 1970s. Introduce the company first: Exxon, since 1999 ExxonMobil, the successor of Rockefeller’s Standard Oil, for decades the largest publicly traded oil company in the world. The story became public through the InsideClimate News series “Exxon: The Road Not Taken” (2015, Pulitzer finalist, https://www.pulitzer.org/finalists/insideclimate-news) and the hashtag #ExxonKnew on the sign.
What the company knew: Supran, Rahmstorf & Oreskes 2023, Science, DOI 10.1126/science.abk0063, evaluated “all available global warming projections documented by—and in many cases modeled by—Exxon and ExxonMobil Corp scientists between 1977 and 2003. We find that most of their projections accurately forecast warming that is consistent with subsequent observations. Their projections were also consistent with, and at least as skillful as, those of independent academic and government models.” In numbers: “63 to 83% of the climate projections reported by ExxonMobil scientists were accurate”, average projected warming “0.20° ± 0.04°C per decade”, warming predicted to become detectable “in the year 2000 ± 5”.
The 1982 internal memo with the CO2 projection chart is at https://www.climatefiles.com/exxonmobil/1982-memo-to-exxon-management-about-CO2-greenhouse-effect. Tobia’s slides 9 and 10 quote three Exxon documents (1977, 1982, 1997) in French. I did not verify their English wording, so they are not on the slide.
Supran & Oreskes 2017, Environmental Research Letters, DOI 10.1088/1748-9326/aa815f, documents from 1977 to 2014. Abstract: “83% of peer-reviewed papers and 80% of internal documents acknowledge that climate change is real and human-caused”, while for advertorials 12% acknowledge this and 81% express doubt.
The quote is from the outlook paragraph of Supran, Rahmstorf & Oreskes 2023: “ExxonMobil didn’t just know ‘something’ about global warming decades ago—they knew as much as academic and government scientists knew. But whereas those scientists worked to communicate what they knew, ExxonMobil worked to deny it—including overemphasizing uncertainties, denigrating climate models, mythologizing global cooling, feigning ignorance about the discernibility of human-caused warming, and staying silent about the possibility of stranded fossil fuel assets in a carbon-constrained world.”

title: Climate change misinformation
section: The side effect: scepticism towards true news
text:
The side effect: scepticism towards true news
Fact-checks, media literacy tips and news coverage of misinformation were tested in the United States, Poland and Hong Kong with 6,127 participants. (Hoes et al., 2024)

“While all interventions successfully reduce belief in false information, they also negatively impact the credibility of factual information.”


Making people more sceptical is easy. Making them better at telling true from false is the hard part.

Hoes, Aitken, Zhang, Gackowski & Wojcieszak 2024, Nature Human Behaviour, DOI 10.1038/s41562-024-01884-x. Abstract: “Current interventions to combat misinformation, including fact-checking, media literacy tips and media coverage of misinformation, may have unintended consequences for democracy. We propose that these interventions may increase scepticism towards all information, including accurate information. Across three online survey experiments in three diverse countries (the United States, Poland and Hong Kong; total n = 6,127), we tested the negative spillover effects of existing strategies and compared them with three alternative interventions against misinformation. We examined how exposure to fact-checking, media literacy tips and media coverage of misinformation affects individuals’ perception of both factual and false information, as well as their trust in key democratic institutions. Our results show that while all interventions successfully reduce belief in false information, they also negatively impact the credibility of factual information.”
The same point comes back in the debate about inoculation games on the next slide: an intervention that lowers belief in everything looks successful if you only measure belief in false news. Emma Hoes’s related work: media attention to misinformation can itself undermine trust in scientists (Hoes et al. 2025, Political Behavior, DOI 10.1007/s11109-025-10090-y). A few slides on comes one way out: tips that build trust in reliable news.

title: Climate change misinformation
section: Who is vulnerable? Putting it together
text:
Who is vulnerable? Putting it together
A meta-analysis of 31 experiments with 11,561 US participants: people judged both true (69%) and false (67%) headlines well above chance. (Sultan et al., 2024)

Older age, higher analytical thinking and identifying as a Democrat went with a better ability to tell true from false news.


News that fitted one’s ideology, and news that felt familiar, went with naïvety: a tendency to call news true.


Showing the source next to the headline improved judgements, most for Republicans.

Sultan, Tump, Ehmann, Lorenz-Spreen, Hertwig, Gollwitzer & Kurvers 2024, PNAS, DOI 10.1073/pnas.2409329121. Abstract: “we conducted a systematic individual participant data meta-analysis covering 256,337 unique choices made by 11,561 US-based participants across 31 experiments. […] We also disentangle the ability to discern between true and false news (discrimination ability) from response bias, that is, the tendency to label news as either true (true-news bias) or false (false-news bias). Across all studies, participants were well above-chance accurate for both true (68.51%) and false (67.24%) news headlines. We find that older age, higher analytical thinking skills, and identifying as a Democrat are associated with higher discrimination ability. Additionally, older age and higher analytical thinking skills are associated with a false-news bias (caution). In contrast, ideological congruency (alignment of participants’ ideology with news), motivated reflection (higher analytical thinking skills being associated with a greater congruency effect), and self-reported familiarity with news are associated with a true-news bias (naïvety). […] Displaying sources alongside news headlines is associated with improved discrimination ability, with Republicans benefiting more from source display.”
Two things to point out. First, the apparent contradiction with the previous slide: older adults share the most fake news (Guess et al. 2019) but judge headlines more accurately here. Sharing and believing are different things (the “disconnect” in Pennycook & Rand 2021), and older adults’ sharing may have social rather than epistemic motives (Brashier & Schacter 2020). Second, the meta-analysis confirms both camps of the “lazy or biased” slide: analytical thinking helps (lazy), and ideological congruency produces a true-news bias (biased), with the two interacting (“motivated reflection”). All US data, which matters for the partisan findings.

title: Climate change misinformation
text:
Poll
What share of what people consume online is misinformation, according to studies that measure actual behaviour (browsing histories, feeds)?

less than 2%
2 to 10%
10 to 25%
more than 25%

title: Climate change misinformation
text:
How much misinformation is there?
A review of 443 studies found that, in the studies that measured actual behaviour, misinformation is a median 1.3% of what people consume online. (Altay, 2026)

Asked in surveys, however, 58% of respondents say they have seen misinformation. (Altay, 2026)

The top 1% of users account for 70% of misinformation sharing or exposure. (Altay, 2026)
Altay 2026, systematic review. The 443 studies include surveys and content analyses. The 1.3% is from the behavioural studies only. Abstract: “In behavioural studies, misinformation is a median 1.3% of what people consume online; it reaches 12.0% of people at least once and makes up 13.0% of what they share. In surveys, 57.7% say they have seen misinformation and 19.8% say they have shared it. In content analyses, 23.0% of items are classified as misinformation. How misinformation was identified (by fact-checkers, domain lists, researchers, or classifiers) and at which level (sources or items) explained more of the variance between estimates than what the study was about; platform and topic explained less. […] The top 1% of users account for a median 70% of misinformation sharing or exposure.”
Earlier single studies pointing the same way (Allen et al., 2020; Grinberg et al., 2019; A. Guess et al., 2019). Grinberg et al. 2019, Science (Twitter, 2016 US election): “Only 1% of individuals accounted for 80% of fake news source exposures, and 0.1% accounted for nearly 80% of fake news sources shared.” Guess, Nagler & Tucker 2019, Science Advances (Facebook): “8.5% of respondents for whom we have linked Facebook data shared at least one such article”, and “users over 65 shared nearly seven times as many articles from fake news domains as the youngest age group”. Allen et al. 2020, Science Advances: “fake news comprises only 0.15% of Americans’ daily media diet”.
The famous counter-example is Vosoughi, Roy & Aral 2018, Science (Vosoughi et al., 2018): on Twitter “falsehoods were 70% more likely to be retweeted than the truth”. Altay, Berriche & Acerbi 2023 (Altay et al., 2023) list as one of six misconceptions that “falsehoods do not spread faster than the truth”: the Vosoughi sample was fact-checked stories, which are selected for being contested, not a random sample of true and false content.
Budak, Nyhan, Rothschild, Thorson & Watts 2024, Nature, DOI 10.1038/s41586-024-07417-w, review the same literature and describe “a pattern of low exposure to false and inflammatory content that is concentrated among a narrow fringe” with strong motivations to seek it out (Budak et al., 2024).
Most of these estimates come from the US and concern fact-checked “fake news”. The next slides say what that leaves out.

title: Climate change misinformation
text:
What these counts miss
Most prevalence studies count fake news from fringe websites. Misleading claims by politicians, think tanks and mainstream outlets are usually not counted. (U. K. H. Ecker et al., 2025)

For climate change, the organised supply from Part I is exactly what these counts miss.


Nor do they count false balance, when journalists give a contrarian the same weight as the scientific consensus. Today’s reading calls this “one of the most insidious, albeit sometimes inadvertent, forms of climate misinformation”. (Lewandowsky, 2021)

Ecker et al. 2025, American Psychologist, DOI 10.1037/amp0001448. Abstract: “the prevalence of misinformation is nonnegligible if reasonably inclusive definitions are applied”. Their companion comment, Ecker et al. 2024, Nature, DOI 10.1038/d41586-024-01587-3 (U. Ecker et al., 2024): “the fight against misinformation is valid, warranted and urgently required.”
The first sentence of the slide is my synthesis of the definitional point: the studies behind the 1.3% identify misinformation through fact-checkers, domain lists or classifiers, which capture fringe fake news well and elite misinformation poorly (Altay et al. 2026 show that how misinformation was identified explains more of the variance between estimates than the topic).
Lewandowsky 2021, section 3.2.1, on false balance: media coverage that gives contrarian voices equal weight “constitutes one of the most insidious, albeit sometimes inadvertent, forms of climate misinformation”. A fake-news count does not see it. Part III returns to the media.

title: Climate change misinformation
text:
One study, both questions
Tobia Spampatti and colleagues tested six inoculation strategies on 6,816 participants in 12 countries. Afterwards, participants read twenty pieces of real-world climate disinformation. (Spampatti et al., 2023)

The six strategies: scientific consensus, trust in scientists, transparent communication, moralisation of climate action, accuracy, positive emotions.


The study answers two questions at once: what does exposure to disinformation do, and does inoculation protect against it?

Spampatti, Hahnel, Trutnevyte & Brosch 2023, Nature Human Behaviour. Abstract: “In a large-scale preregistered experiment (N = 6,816), we tested six inoculation strategies […] across twelve countries”. The six strategies are named in the abstract: “protecting the scientific consensus, trust in scientists, transparent communication, moralization of climate action, accuracy, and positive emotions”. Participants were then “exposed to twenty real-world climate disinformation statements”. A control group read no disinformation, which is what makes the exposure effect measurable.
Why this study: the earlier inoculation studies measured recognition of techniques or belief in a single counter-message. This one uses real climate disinformation, many countries, and behaviour as an outcome.

title: Climate change misinformation
text:
Two results

Exposure to the disinformation lowered belief in climate change, made people feel less positive about reducing emissions, and reduced pro-environmental behaviour.



Inoculation strategies hardly helped prevent this.



“While exposure to disinformation had strong detrimental effects […], we found almost no evidence for protective effects of the inoculations.” (Spampatti et al., 2023)

Abstract: “exposure to disinformation had strong detrimental effects on participants’ climate change beliefs (δ = −0.16), affect towards climate mitigation action (δ = −0.33), ability to detect disinformation (δ = −0.14) and pro-environmental behaviour (δ = −0.24)”. The behaviour measure was trees planted via completed pages of a task. By convention these effects are small to moderate, after twenty statements read in one sitting and measured right away.
La Selva et al. 2026 on this study: “the protective effect of the accuracy message was evident at the onset of the intervention but diminished when multiple false news items were presented consecutively”, and “climate misinformation exerts a powerful and resilient influence due to repeated exposure, which remains difficult to counteract even when targeted psychological interventions are applied.” The review also classes the study as “general prebunking” (accuracy, consensus, trust and similar messages). Three of the 14 studies were general prebunking, the other 11 used specific inoculation strategies.
Two results matter for Part III: disinformation does something when people read it, and one short inoculation message did little against twenty pieces of it.

title: Climate change misinformation
text:
Worldview first
Across 56 nations, when predicting belief in climate change, education, knowledge and experience of extreme weather were “overshadowed in predictive power by values, ideologies, worldviews and political orientation”. (Hornsey et al., 2016)

The same holds for climate misinformation. In eight countries on four continents, identifying as right-wing and distrusting scientists were among the strongest predictors of believing false claims about climate change. (Ejaz, Altay, et al., 2025)


Today’s reading: climate change “challenges our cognitive abilities and the worldviews of many”. (Lewandowsky, 2021)

Ejaz et al. 2025, New Media & Society, DOI 10.1177/14614448241250302, N = 8,541 in the US, France, Germany, the UK, Japan, Brazil, India and Pakistan. Abstract: “Across countries, we found that the strongest determinants of belief in misinformation about climate change were identifying as right-wing (compared with left-wing), consuming less offline news, having less trust in scientists, environmental activists, as well as international organizations, and having more trust in politicians, celebrities, and energy companies.”
Berkebile-Weinberg et al. 2024, Nature Communications, DOI 10.1038/s41467-024-48112-8, abstract: “In a global experiment conducted in 60 countries (N = 51,224) […] At baseline, we find political polarization of climate change beliefs and policy support globally, with people who reported being liberal believing and supporting climate policy more than those who reported being conservative (Cohen’s d = 0.35 and 0.27, respectively).”
Hornsey, Harris, Bain & Fielding 2016, Nature Climate Change, DOI 10.1038/nclimate2943. Abstract: “Twenty-seven variables were examined by synthesizing 25 polls and 171 academic studies across 56 nations”, and the demographic and experience variables were “overshadowed in predictive power by values, ideologies, worldviews and political orientation.” Mostly US and Western data, polarisation is weaker elsewhere.
Lewandowsky, Woike & Oberauer 2021, Cognition. Abstract: “U.S. surveys have repeatedly shown that the rejection of scientific evidence across a broad range of domains is preferentially associated with rightwing or libertarian worldviews […] Both studies show that people’s political worldviews are associated with their attitudes towards those scientific norms, and that those attitudes predict people’s acceptance of vaccinations and climate science.”
Lewandowsky 2021, summary point 1: “Climate change challenges our cognitive abilities and the worldviews of many.” Section 2 adds the cognitive side: the power of anecdotes (Inhofe’s snowball, local temperature shaping beliefs) and the stock-and-flow problem (the bathtub from week 4). Link to Part I: the Luntz memo and the think-tank material were aimed at exactly this audience.

title: Climate change misinformation
text:
Putting it together
A meta-analysis of 31 experiments with 11,561 US participants: people judged both true (69%) and false (67%) headlines well above chance. (Sultan et al., 2024)

Older age, higher analytical thinking and identifying as a Democrat went with a better ability to tell true from false news.

Sultan, Tump, Ehmann, Lorenz-Spreen, Hertwig, Gollwitzer & Kurvers 2024, PNAS, DOI 10.1073/pnas.2409329121. Abstract: “we conducted a systematic individual participant data meta-analysis covering 256,337 unique choices made by 11,561 US-based participants across 31 experiments. […] We also disentangle the ability to discern between true and false news (discrimination ability) from response bias, that is, the tendency to label news as either true (true-news bias) or false (false-news bias). Across all studies, participants were well above-chance accurate for both true (68.51%) and false (67.24%) news headlines. We find that older age, higher analytical thinking skills, and identifying as a Democrat are associated with higher discrimination ability. Additionally, older age and higher analytical thinking skills are associated with a false-news bias (caution). In contrast, ideological congruency (alignment of participants’ ideology with news), motivated reflection (higher analytical thinking skills being associated with a greater congruency effect), and self-reported familiarity with news are associated with a true-news bias (naïvety). […] Displaying sources alongside news headlines is associated with improved discrimination ability, with Republicans benefiting more from source display.”
Two things to point out. First, the apparent contradiction with the previous slide: older adults share the most fake news (Guess et al. 2019) but judge headlines more accurately here. Sharing and believing are different things (the “disconnect” in Pennycook & Rand 2021), and older adults’ sharing may have social rather than epistemic motives (Brashier & Schacter 2020). Second, the meta-analysis confirms both camps of the “lazy or biased” slide: analytical thinking helps (lazy), and ideological congruency produces a true-news bias (biased), with the two interacting (“motivated reflection”). All US data, which matters for the partisan findings.

title: Climate change misinformation
section: Has the supply of doubt worked?
text:
Has the supply of doubt worked?
In the EU, the share who say it is true that “climate change is for the most part caused by natural cycles rather than human activities” rose from 26% in 2021 to 35% in 2024. (European Commission, Directorate-General for Research and Innovation, 2021, 2025)

In Switzerland, 37% find it plausible that governments use climate change as a pretext to control the population. (Fög, 2026)


Is misinformation the cause? The question is harder than it looks.

fög Jahrbuch Qualität der Medien 2026 (published 26 October 2026), from the UZH press release (https://www.news.uzh.ch/de/articles/media/2026/JB_foeg_2026.html): “Grundlage ist eine repräsentative Onlinebefragung von 1222 Personen in der Deutschschweiz und der Suisse romande.” “37% halten es für eher oder sehr plausibel, dass Regierungen den Klimawandel als Vorwand nutzen, um die Bevölkerung zu kontrollieren.” Also: “Wer private Qualitätsmedien mit Angeboten des Service Public kombiniert oder journalistisch produzierte Nachrichten in Radio und Fernsehen nutzt, ist weniger anfällig für desinformative Verschwörungsaussagen” (correlational).
Eurobarometer, “European citizens’ knowledge and attitudes towards science and technology”, 2021 (DOI 10.2775/071577) and Special Eurobarometer 557, 2025 (DOI 10.2777/6040908). The item is a true/false knowledge question, “Climate change is for the most part caused by natural cycles rather than human activities” (correct answer: false). Special Eurobarometer 516, fieldwork April to May 2021, p. 62: “A quarter of respondents (26%) incorrectly say that the statement is true”, 65% correctly say false, 9% don’t know. Special Eurobarometer 557, fieldwork September to October 2024, p. 33: “More than a third of respondents (35%, +9 pp) incorrectly say that the statement is true”, 58% (−7 pp) correctly say false, 7% don’t know. In 2024, more than half say true in Poland (52%), Czechia, Slovakia and Hungary (all 51%), p. 36. Switzerland was 75% correct in 2021 (p. 65).
Rutjens et al. 2022, Social Psychological and Personality Science, DOI 10.1177/19485506211001329, “Science skepticism across 24 countries”: climate scepticism was related to political conservatism mostly in North America, and spirituality and religiosity predicted other forms of scepticism (vaccines, evolution) in more countries.

title: Climate change misinformation
text:
Misinformation does something
Today’s reading: “Misinformation demonstrably undermines the public’s knowledge and acceptance of climate change.” (Lewandowsky, 2021)

The IPCC: misinformation “has created polarisation in public and policy domains in North America, particularly in the USA, limiting climate action (high confidence)”. (Hicke et al., 2022)


And in the case study, reading twenty pieces of disinformation lowered beliefs, affect and behaviour, by small to moderate amounts.

Lewandowsky 2021, section 3.2.2: “Misinformation demonstrably undermines the public’s knowledge and acceptance of climate change. Just a handful of misleading numbers often used by ‘skeptics’ can lower acceptance of climate change. Misinformation can also cancel out the impact of accurate information. When people are presented with two conflicting pieces of information, the two can cancel each other out.” Abstract: “an environment of rhetorical adversity in which disinformation abounds”.
Hicke et al. 2022, IPCC AR6 WGII, Chapter 14 (North America), Executive Summary, p. 1931 (https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg2/chapter/chapter-14/): “misinformation and politicisation of climate-change science has created polarisation in public and policy domains in North America, particularly in the USA, limiting climate action (high confidence). Vested interests have generated rhetoric and misinformation that undermines climate science and disregards risk and urgency (medium confidence). Resultant public misperception of climate risks and polarised public support for climate actions is delaying urgent adaptation planning and implementation (high confidence).” Not in the Summary for Policymakers, only in the chapter.
Spampatti et al. 2023: δ = −0.16 (beliefs), −0.33 (affect), −0.24 (behaviour), see section 5.
So exposure has effects in experiments. The next three slides ask whether fooling people is the mechanism in the real world.

title: Climate change misinformation
section: But people are not easily fooled
text:
But people are not easily fooled
Across 67 experimental papers from 40 countries, people rated true news as much more accurate than fact-checked false news. When they made mistakes, they more often doubted true news than believed false news. (Pfänder & Altay, 2025)

Political congruence did not change how well people told true from false news. It made them more sceptical of news from the other side, true or false.


Most people say they would have to be paid to share fake news. (Altay et al., 2022)

Pfänder & Altay 2025, Nature Human Behaviour, DOI 10.1038/s41562-024-02086-1. Abstract: “We conducted a systematic literature review and pre-registered meta-analysis of 303 effect sizes from 67 experimental articles evaluating accuracy ratings of true and fact-checked false news (NParticipants = 194,438 from 40 countries across 6 continents). We found that people rated true news as more accurate than false news (Cohen’s d = 1.12 [1.01, 1.22]) and were better at rating false news as false than at rating true news as true (Cohen’s d = 0.32 [0.24, 0.39]). […] We found no evidence that the political concordance of the news had an effect on discernment, but participants were more skeptical of politically discordant news (Cohen’s d = 0.78 [0.62, 0.94]).” This is my own work, say so. The congruence result: discernment was the same for politically concordant and discordant news, but people gave lower accuracy ratings to discordant news overall, so worldview shows up as extra doubt about news from the other side, true and false alike, and not as gullibility for one’s own side. Our conclusion: “there is more room to increase the acceptance of true news than to reduce the acceptance of fact-checked false news.”
Altay, Hacquin & Mercier 2022, New Media & Society, N = 3,656. Abstract: “sharing fake news hurt one’s reputation in a way that is difficult to fix, even for politically congruent fake news. […] the majority of people declare they would have to be paid to share fake news”.

title: Climate change misinformation
text:
Trust, rather than exposure
In eight countries, how much people trusted their sources of information about climate change predicted belief in climate misinformation much better than how much news they consumed. (Ejaz, Altay, et al., 2025)

Across 56 nations, values, worldviews and political orientation predicted belief in climate change better than education, knowledge or experience. (Hornsey et al., 2016)

Ejaz, Altay, Fletcher & Nielsen 2025, New Media & Society, DOI 10.1177/14614448241250302: “online survey (N = 8541)”; “trust in sources of information about climate change and demographic variables were much stronger predictors of belief in misinformation about climate change than reported news consumption”. This connects to week 3 on trust.
Hornsey et al. 2016. The point of putting the two together: who believes climate misinformation is explained by trust and worldview, which are not things a fact-check changes.

title: Climate change misinformation
section: Why individual-level interventions will not fix this
text:
Why individual-level interventions will not fix this
The effects of debunking, prebunking and accuracy prompts are real but modest, measured minutes after the intervention, and they decay within weeks. (Capewell et al., 2024; Fazio et al., 2024; Maertens et al., 2021)

Against twenty pieces of real climate disinformation, six inoculation strategies did almost nothing. (Spampatti et al., 2023)

Callbacks to section 5 (Fazio et al. 2024: nine interventions, 33,233 participants, effects measured immediately; Maertens et al. 2021: decay within two months without reminders; Capewell et al. 2024: d = 0.416 with an immediate post-test, d = 0.010 without) and section 5 (Spampatti et al. 2023).
Before the costs, the scaling problem: two slides on whether correction can reach people at all, and whether AI changes that. Then the side effects.

title: Climate change misinformation
section: Trust in news is low in most countries
text:
Trust in news is low in most countries

Newman et al. (2019)
Reuters Institute Digital News Report 2019, p. 21, chart “Proportion that trust most news most of the time, all markets” (fieldwork early 2019). Report text: “Trust is down 11 points in Brazil after the recent fractious election, but perhaps the biggest surprise is a 11-point fall in trust in France from 35% to 24%, driven by the partisan nature of the Yellow Vest protests.” Finland 59%, Switzerland 46%, Germany 47%, USA 32%, France 24%, South Korea 22%. Most markets are below half.
Update from the 2026 report (Egan et al., 2026), executive summary: “Having held steady at 40% for three years, the percentage of people globally saying they trust news overall dropped to 37%, the lowest figure since we started measuring trust in 2015. Out of our 48 markets, 29 reported significant falls in trust in news this year”. Switzerland page (read 2026-11-09): “Trust in news overall 42% (-4)”, French-speaking 37%, German-speaking 45%, “Global average: 37%”. The report’s text: “Overall trust levels tend to fluctuate and are currently slightly lower than in 2025.”
Why this matters here: people err towards doubting true news, as the previous slide showed. Most news is true, and people do not trust it much. The 2026 Swiss page also notes the SRG SSR referendum debate on halving the licence fee, which is a Swiss version of the next slides.

title: Climate change misinformation
section: And interest in news is falling
text:
And interest in news is falling

Newman et al. (2024)
Update from the 2026 report (Egan et al., 2026): interest in news fell “from 59% to just under 46%” since 2021 across markets.
Reuters Institute Digital News Report 2024, chart “Proportion extremely or very interested in news (2015–2024)”, selected countries. Read from the chart: UK 70% to 38%, France 59% to 36%, Germany 74% to 55%, Spain 85% to 52%, USA 67% to 52%, Finland 64% to 65%.
Falling trust and falling interest are the demand side of a weaker news environment. After the next slide comes the supply side.

title: Climate change misinformation
text:
The economics of news





Cagé (2016)



“There have never been as many information producers as there are today. Paradoxically, the media have never been in worse shape.” (Cagé, 2016)


Julia Cagé, economist at Sciences Po Paris, Saving the Media: Capitalism, Crowdfunding, and Democracy (Harvard University Press, 2016, French original Sauver les médias, Seuil 2015). The quote is from the excerpt adapted from the book in Nieman Reports (“News is a public good”, https://niemanreports.org/news-is-a-public-good/), verbatim: “There have never been as many information producers as there are today. Paradoxically, the media have never been in worse shape”. Her diagnosis in that text: newspapers cutting staff (Libération lost a third of its staff in early 2015), papers bought and shut down by chains (E.W. Scripps), and a growing dependence on wealthy investors.
Angelucci & Cagé 2019, AEJ: Microeconomics, DOI 10.1257/mic.20170306. Abstract: “We show that a reduction in advertising revenues lowers newspapers’ incentives to produce journalistic-intensive content. We also build a unique dataset on French newspapers between 1960 and 1974 and perform a difference-in-differences analysis exploiting the introduction of advertising on television, which affected national newspapers more severely than local ones. We find robust evidence of a decrease in the amount of journalistic-intensive content produced and the subscription price.” The slide sentence is a paraphrase of the model’s mechanism: journalistic-intensive content is the expensive part.
Cagé, Hervé & Viaud 2020, Review of Economic Studies, DOI 10.1093/restud/rdz061. Abstract: “we build a unique dataset combining all the online content produced by French news media during the year 2013”; “one quarter of the news stories are reproduced online in under 4 min. We show that this is accompanied by substantial copying, both at the extensive and at the intensive margins, which may constitute a severe threat to the commercial viability of the news media.” They also find that “original content producers tend to receive more viewers”, which mitigates the problem.

title: Climate change misinformation
text:
Who owns the news?



Owner
Newspaper




Jeff Bezos, founder of Amazon
The Washington Post


John Henry, owner of the Boston Red Sox
The Boston Globe


Patrick Soon-Shiong, biotech billionaire
Los Angeles Times


Christoph Blocher, former Swiss justice minister
Basler Zeitung



Melley (2018); “Newspaper Takeover Reveals Rightwing Strategy” (2011)

Melley 2018, Associated Press, in The Boston Globe, 7 February 2018: “A biotech billionaire struck a $500 million deal Wednesday to buy the Los Angeles Times […] With the newspaper industry thrown into deep turmoil by the internet, Amazon founder Jeff Bezos bought The Washington Post in 2013 for $250 million. The same year, Boston Red Sox owner John Henry purchased The Boston Globe for $70 million.” Al Tompkins of the Poynter Institute, in the same article: “We find ourselves returning to where we were a century ago when a handful of wealthy owners controlled big, influential newspapers. Here’s the difference: The ownership today does not promise lucrative returns. You take it over knowing it isn’t nearly as profitable as it might have been 20 or 50 years ago.”
swissinfo.ch, 13 December 2011: “Moritz Suter, founder of the airline Crossair, bought the Basler Zeitung’s parent company Basler Zeitung Media around a year ago and became president of the board of directors. Behind him, despite their denials, was billionaire businessman and former Justice Minister Christoph Blocher and his daughter. […] He fronted the SFr70 million ($74 million) loan from Blocher to Suter. Ultimately, because of differences in opinion in how the company should be restructured, the Blochers exercised the option to claim Suter’s shares”. In 2018 the Basler Zeitung went to Tamedia, in exchange for free local papers that went to Blocher’s Zeitungshaus AG (swissinfo.ch, 11 October 2018, “Tamedia given green light to buy Basler Zeitung”).

title: Climate change misinformation
text:
What follows
Interventions that protect individuals from misinformation help somewhat, but they miss the bigger picture.

To keep the zone from being flooded, we need strong and independent journalism that people trust and actually use.


Platforms and the organised supply of doubt from Part I remain part of the problem. (Budak et al., 2024)

Altay, De Angelis & Hoes 2024, Communications Psychology, N = 3,919. Abstract: “Skepticism-enhancing tips, Trust-inducing tips, and a mix of both tips, increased participants’ sharing and accuracy discernment. […] the Trust-inducing tips increased trust in traditional media.”
On the supply: Michael Mann’s defamation suit from the opening took twelve years and ended in a symbolic award, so the individual route is costly. Regulation of funding transparency and advertising is the collective one.
On the third lever: Cagé’s nonprofit media organisation is one proposal. Week 3 covered trust in scientists. Today’s reading, summary point 3: information about the consensus and about why climate change occurs enhances acceptance of science, which is building trust in true information rather than fighting false information.
Budak et al. 2024: “we recommend holding platforms accountable for facilitating exposure to false and extreme content in the tails of the distribution, where consumption is highest and the risk of real-world harm is greatest.”

title: Climate change misinformation
section: Another way to do harm: flooding
text:
Another way to do harm: flooding
“Disinformation strategies are often deployed by professionals to elicit confusion rather than to persuade.” (Szegőfi et al., 2027)

In two experiments, a flooded information environment pushed “the evaluation of information into the realm of uncertainty” and increased feelings of information overload.


Steve Bannon, 2018: “The real opposition is the media. And the way to deal with them is to flood the zone with shit.” (Lewis, 2018)

Szegőfi, Altay & Heintz, British Journal of Social Psychology, DOI 10.1111/bjso.70151, online 8 November 2026. Abstract: “Disinformation strategies are often deployed by professionals to elicit confusion rather than to persuade. One key method for this is ‘flooding’: inserting a large number of incongruent propositions into the communication environment, with the goal of preventing people from identifying and acting on reliable information. We assess some of the basic elements of this strategy with two pre-registered experimental studies (N = 2607) on the topics of sunscreens and GMOs. We pitted a flooded versus a non-flooded information environment against each other, with varying levels of accurate and inaccurate propositions. Our findings suggest that, in some cases, flooding can influence attitudes, push the evaluation of information into the realm of uncertainty and increase subjective feelings of information overload. We further speculate that flooding may elicit rational inattention and have other downstream consequences such as fatigue and passivity.” Sacha Altay is a co-author, say so.
The point for the argument: the previous slide showed that people are not easily persuaded of specific false claims. Flooding does not need to persuade. It needs people to give up on telling reliable from unreliable information. That is the Luntz strategy from Part I (“make the lack of scientific certainty a primary issue”) and the tobacco logic of manufacturing doubt, scaled up. It also fits the Nohlen result in section 4: the persuasion techniques lowered agreement with true claims rather than raising agreement with false ones.
Bannon quote: Michael Lewis, “Has Anyone Seen the President?”, Bloomberg View, 9 February 2018, on watching the State of the Union with Steve Bannon. The passage as quoted by Political Wire the same day (https://politicalwire.com/2018/02/09/through-bannons-eyes/): “‘The Democrats don’t matter,’ he had said to me over our lunch. ‘The real opposition is the media. And the way to deal with them is to flood the zone with shit.’” Column URL: https://www.bloomberg.com/view/articles/2018-02-09/has-anyone-seen-the-president (paywalled). The Bloomberg page itself refused automated access, so the wording was checked against the Political Wire excerpt only. Brian Stelter’s CNN piece of 16 November 2021 on the quote reports Jonathan Rauch’s gloss “This is not about persuasion: This is about disorientation”, which is the flooding argument in one line (seen only in a search snippet, check before quoting). The quote is about politics and the media in general, not climate. Soften the last word orally if you prefer.

title: Climate change misinformation
text:
How doubt is manufactured
Oreskes and Conway stress that nothing in this story was illegal or hidden. The campaigns were run in the open, by scientists with political connections and a conviction that environmental regulation would lead to socialism. (Oreskes & Conway, 2010)

Concretely: reports outside peer review that reached the White House, a petition of “scientists” against the consensus, and above all appeals to fairness and balance that won a fringe view equal time in the media.


The same people had earlier questioned the evidence on tobacco, acid rain and the ozone hole. The Exxon advertorial on the previous slide used the same move: a real result, taken out of context, presented as if nothing were settled.

Source check (2026-11-09): the slide rests on the authors’ own FAQ at merchantsofdoubt.org, the book itself was not consulted. FAQ: “As far as we know, none of the players in our story did anything illegal, and it was all done quite openly. The men in our story had dedicated their lives to science and technology in the cause of defending the U.S. against the Soviet threat. When the Cold War ended just a few years later, they just couldn’t lay down their arms. So they found a new threat in environmentalism, which they worried would lead to excessive government regulation of the marketplace, and put us on the slippery slope to socialism.” On the media: “A key tactic used by the Merchants of Doubt was to invoke the ideals of fairness and balance to persuade the media to give equal time to their views.” On the trajectory: “some of the people who were challenging the scientific evidence of global warming had previously questioned the evidence of stratospheric ozone depletion and the harms of tobacco. Then we found evidence connecting them to the tobacco industry”. Acid rain is one of the book’s chapters and, per the Wikipedia page on the Marshall Institute, among the issues on which it cast doubt.
The report that reached the White House: the 1990 Marshall Institute report by Jastrow, Nierenberg and Seitz, which informed the first Bush administration’s position (Wikipedia, Marshall Institute). The petition: see the Oregon Petition note below. The last sentence links back to the Keigwin graph in the “Unsettled Science” advertorial (Supran & Oreskes 2017).
(Global Warming Petition Project), circulated from 1998 and again in 2007, which asked the US government to reject the Kyoto agreement: “There is no convincing scientific evidence that human release of carbon dioxide, methane, or other greenhouse gases is causing or will, in the foreseeable future, cause catastrophic heating of the Earth’s atmosphere” (petition card as reproduced in Viktoria Cologna’s UZH deck, week 4, slide 18). The project’s site claims 31,487 American scientists as signatories, 9,029 with PhDs, with no requirement of any climate expertise. Cook’s chapter uses it as the textbook case of fake experts. I could not reach the site to verify the current count, so do not put the number on a slide without checking.
